title: Elegant Kitchen Renovations with Marble Countertops
meta: Marble countertops etch, stain and need sealing, yet nothing else looks like them. Wills Flooring's guide to honed vs polished, care and who should choose it.
keywords: marble countertops kitchen, marble countertop pros and cons, honed vs polished marble, does marble etch, marble countertop sealing, kitchen remodel Edmonds countertops

blocks.lead: Marble gives a kitchen a look nothing engineered can copy, and in exchange it etches, stains and wears. Choose it if you will enjoy the patina; skip it if you want the counter to look new in ten years.
blocks.detail: Wills Flooring installs marble on kitchen remodels from Edmonds to Seattle and prices every top from a measured template, so there is no per-foot number here. What follows is what we tell customers before they fall in love with a slab.

blocks.html: Marble is the counter people ask about after seeing it in a Seattle Craftsman kitchen or a Queen Anne remodel, and then talk themselves out of after reading a forum thread about lemon juice. Both reactions are correct. Marble is the most beautiful surface you can put in a kitchen and the most demanding. This post explains the trade exactly, so you can make it on purpose.

blocks.text: Why marble still wins on looks

items.title: Depth you cannot print
items.text: Marble is slightly translucent. Light goes into the stone and comes back out, which is why a white marble kitchen glows on a gray Edmonds afternoon in a way no quartz manages. The veining is unique to your slab.

items.title: It fits older houses
items.text: In 1910s to 1950s kitchens in Seattle, Shoreline and Everett, marble reads as original in a way engineered stone never does. It is also right for the farmhouse and Scandinavian looks that dominate Puget Sound remodels.

items.title: Range of stone
items.text: Bright whites with gray veins, softer creams, greens and dramatic dark grays. Some quarries produce denser, more forgiving stone than others; ask the fabricator which slabs they see fewer problems with.

items.title: Resale in the right market
items.text: In Seattle, Kirkland and the Edmonds Bowl, a well-kept marble kitchen photographs better than anything else and buyers respond. In a mid-priced Lynnwood or Bothell remodel, quartz returns about the same money with less worry.

blocks.text: Etching is not staining: what actually happens

blocks.html: Marble is calcium carbonate, and acid dissolves it. A lemon wedge left on the counter for ten minutes leaves a dull spot in the polish, called an etch. That is not a stain, and no sealer prevents it; sealer only slows liquids from soaking in. Understanding that difference is most of learning to live with marble.

items.title: Honed (matte)
items.text: Ground smooth but not shined. Etches are far less visible because there is no gloss for acid to dull. It feels soft and chalky, hides fingerprints, and is what we recommend for a working kitchen. Slightly more prone to staining, so sealing matters more.

items.title: Polished (gloss)
items.text: The classic shining surface, deepest in color and most reflective. Every etch shows as a dull spot in the shine. It stains a little less because the pores are tighter. Best where acids are rare: bathroom vanities, a pantry or a display island.

blocks.text: The sealing schedule and daily care

items.text: The fabricator applies an impregnating sealer. Ask which product so you can match it later.
Wipe with a pH-neutral stone cleaner or plain water. No vinegar, no bleach sprays, no scrub powders.
Water test: drop a few drops on the counter. If they darken the stone within five minutes, reseal.
Reseal the whole surface. Busy kitchens and honed finishes sit at the shorter end.
Have a stone pro re-hone the worst etched areas. It restores the surface without replacing anything.

blocks.html: Marble stays a few degrees cooler than the room because it pulls heat out of whatever touches it. Pastry dough, pie crust and tempered chocolate behave better on it, which is why it has been the pastry surface for centuries. You do not need a whole kitchen of it for that. Many of our customers put a honed marble slab on the baking side of the island and quartz everywhere else, and get the benefit without worrying about the coffee station.

blocks.text: Which rooms, and who should not choose marble

a.title: Good call for
items: Bathroom vanities and shower walls where acids are rare
A baking island or pastry section
Owners who like patina and will reseal on schedule
Period kitchens in older Seattle, Edmonds and Everett homes

b.title: Skip marble when
items: You want a counter that looks new after ten years of family use
Young kids, lemon water and red wine are daily fixtures
Nobody in the house will do the water test or reseal
The kitchen is a rental or a flip; quartz returns the money with no maintenance risk

blocks.text: How to choose a marble slab

items.html: Pick your actual slab at the yard. Two slabs from the same quarry can look like different stones. Ask to see the pair if you want book-matched veining on an island.
Do the lemon test on a sample. Leave a lemon slice on it for 15 minutes and look at the mark. If it bothers you, choose honed, or choose quartz.
Go 3 cm and plan the seams. Thicker marble cracks less across sink cutouts. Have the fabricator lay the template on the slab so a strong vein does not stop dead at a seam.
Mix surfaces on purpose. Marble on the baking run, quartz around the sink and coffee maker. It is common, it looks intentional, and it cuts the maintenance in half.

Get the care plan in writing. Sealer product, resealing interval and who to call for re-honing. Wills Flooring hands this over at install and prices the whole kitchen, tops and floors, in one written quote. Start with a free in-home consultation.

faq.q: Is marble a bad idea for a kitchen countertop?
faq.a: Not bad, but demanding. Marble etches from acids, stains if unsealed and scratches more easily than granite or quartz. If you like a lived-in surface and will reseal every 6 to 12 months, it is wonderful. If you want it to look new in ten years, choose quartz.

faq.q: What is the difference between etching and staining on marble?
faq.a: Etching is acid dissolving the polish, leaving a dull spot; sealer does not prevent it. Staining is a liquid soaking into the pores and leaving color; sealer prevents most of that. Honed marble hides etching, polished marble resists staining a bit better.

faq.q: How often does marble need sealing?
faq.a: Every 6 to 12 months in a working kitchen, less often on a bathroom vanity. Do a water test monthly: if drops darken the stone within five minutes, it is time. Use an impregnating stone sealer and match the product the fabricator used.

faq.q: Honed or polished marble for a kitchen?
faq.a: Honed for almost every kitchen. The matte surface hides etch marks and fingerprints and feels softer. Polished suits bathrooms, a display island or a pantry where acids rarely land. Both need the same sealing schedule.

faq.q: Does marble add value to a home?
faq.a: In upper-end Seattle, Kirkland and Edmonds markets, a well-kept marble kitchen photographs and shows better than any other counter and buyers pay for it. In mid-range Lynnwood or Bothell remodels, quartz returns about the same money with none of the maintenance concerns.

It stays a few degrees cooler than the room and pulls heat out of dough, so butter stays firm and pastry does not stick. You do not need a full marble kitchen; a honed marble slab on one section of the island gives the same benefit.
